title: Catastrophic Forest Fires Burn 430,000 Hectares
reason: Multiple independent sources confirm Portugal suffered a catastrophic wave of forest fires in summer 2003, repeatedly described as the worst in Portugal's modern history up to that point. Area-burned estimates across sources cluster around 425,000-471,750 hectares (one academic source says 'near to 500,000 hectares' of forest/shrub/agricultural land burned), bracketing the event's stated 430,000 figure. Death toll is reported as 18 in tertiary sources (Wikipedia's List of wildfires) but the dedicated academic paper on the disaster ("The Deep Roots of the 2003 Forest Fires in Portugal", Varela, International Forest Fire News 35, 2006) states twenty-one human lives were lost, matching the event description's "at least 21 people" almost exactly. NASA Earth Observatory imagery from Aug 3, 2003 shows the fires actively burning across central Portugal mid-crisis (9 dead at that snapshot, consistent with a rising toll as the season continued). ReliefWeb/EFFIS reports, a EUMETSAT case study, and multiple academic journals (MDPI, ResearchGate-indexed papers) all corroborate the country, year, and unprecedented scale, and describe the ensuing political/policy scrutiny of Portugal's forest management and emergency response -- all materially matching the event description.

verifications.reason: Multiple independent sources confirm Portugal suffered its worst forest-fire season on record in summer 2003. Burned-area figures across sources cluster tightly around the claimed 430,000 ha: 425,839 ha (ECO/Sapo, citing official ICNF-derived data), 425,000-471,750 ha (academic literature via search aggregation), and 355,976 ha mapped by EFFIS as of Aug 20 alone (an undercount, since EFFIS satellite detection only reliably captures burns ≥50ha and the season continued into September). Economic damage of 611 million euros (ECO/Sapo) matches "hundreds of millions of euros." Deaths: most general-audience sources (Wikipedia, ECO/Sapo, EUMETSAT case study) cite 18 fatalities, but a peer-reviewed academic source specifically studying human losses in Portuguese rural fires (MDPI Applied Sciences, "Rural Fires-Causes of Human Losses in the 2017 Fires in Portugal") states 21 deaths in Portugal in 2003 -- matching the event's "at least 21" figure exactly. The spread (18 vs 21) likely reflects different counting windows/methodologies (e.g., direct fire deaths vs. broader fire-related fatalities including firefighters/subsequent injuries), which is a minor, non-material discrepancy given "at least 21" is itself hedged language and is directly attested by a specialized academic source. Country, year, and the core narrative (catastrophic, unprecedented wildfire disaster exposing forest-management/emergency-response deficiencies) are solidly confirmed across ReliefWeb/EFFIS, Portuguese Wikipedia, ECO/Sapo, EUMETSAT, and academic literature.

title: Armed Forces Movement Forms Among Disillusioned Officers
reason: Multiple independent sources (English Wikipedia, Portuguese Wikipedia, and the Associação 25 de Abril historical archive) converge on a well-documented origin story that places the formation of the officers' movement in 1973, not 1970. The proximate trigger was Decree-Law 353/73 (13 July 1973), which let militia officers gain permanent-corps rank via a short course, angering Military Academy graduates. The first clandestine meeting of captains took place in Bissau on 21 August 1973, the first commission of the 'Movimento dos Capitães' was elected 28 August 1973, and a farmhouse meeting of ~163-176 captains in September 1973 (with a formal manifesto in December 1973 and a 5 March 1974 assembly) crystallized it into the Movimento das Forças Armadas (MFA), which then executed the Carnation Revolution on 25 April 1974. No source found any clandestine discontent/discussion groups specifically dating to 1970 that evolved into the MFA — the 'early 1970s' phrasing some sources use refers loosely to the 1973 captains' movement, not an earlier 1970 origin. Country and general substance (disillusioned officers amid the colonial wars forming clandestine groups that became the MFA and planned a coup) are correct, but the year is off by three years.

verifications.reason: Independent sources (English & Portuguese Wikipedia, Infopédia, 50anos25abril.pt) consistently date the formation of this movement to 1973, not 1970. The precursor "Movimento dos Capitães" (Captains' Movement) was triggered by Decree-Law 353/73 (July 1973, on militia-officer commissioning) and formally founded on 9 September 1973 at a clandestine meeting of ~163-300 army captains in Cascais; it broadened into political/anti-colonial-war aims by November 1973 and was renamed Movimento das Forças Armadas (MFA) on 5 March 1974, ahead of the 25 April 1974 Carnation Revolution coup. Nothing in the record supports clandestine discussion groups evolving into the MFA as early as 1970 — the specific catalyst (Decree-Law 353/73) postdates 1970 by three years, and no source describes an MFA-precursor movement forming in 1970. The country (Portugal) and general substance (disillusioned junior/colonial-war officers forming clandestine groups that evolved into the MFA and planned the coup) are materially correct, but the year is off by three years, which the hard rules treat as FALSE (with corrected_year reported).
